title: Why Dropshipping Won't Make You Rich (Even With Sales)

beats.text: Three thousand dollars in sales. Then Dave checked his bank account: he was down one thousand five hundred forty six dollars.
He sold a glowing cat lamp for thirty dollars. He never kept one at home; the supplier shipped each lamp straight to the buyer and charged Dave twelve dollars.
The store dashboard looked amazing. Orders kept coming in, and Dave thought he'd cracked online business. He hadn't counted what each sale cost.
On a thirty-dollar sale, twelve dollars went to the supplier. That left eighteen dollars before payment fees, advertising, refunds, or anything else.
The payment processor took one dollar and twenty cents. Dave had sixteen dollars and eighty cents left to cover ads and every other cost.
Dave paid to advertise the lamp. Each click cost fifty cents, whether someone bought the lamp or scrolled straight past.
One hundred clicks cost fifty dollars. Only two people bought, so Dave spent twenty-five dollars in ads to get each customer.
The ad platform got its fifty dollars. The payment processor got its fee. The supplier got paid. Dave had just sixteen dollars and eighty cents per sale before ads.
Then some lamps arrived late. Customers asked for refunds, and some disputed the charges with their banks. Dave had to deal with those losses too.
Dave grabbed a calculator. Sixteen dollars and eighty cents was the most he could spend to get one customer just to break even, before refunds and other costs.
But each customer cost him twenty-five dollars in ads. That meant a loss of at least eight dollars and twenty cents per sale, before refunds.
Dave turned off the ads and shut the laptop. Three thousand dollars in sales wasn't profit. He had to count every cost before buying another click.
Follow for money stories with the actual numbers. Next, Dave borrows money to rescue a business that's already losing.
